clinicalPearls: Postsynaptic congenital myasthenic syndrome caused by dominant gain-of-function variants in acetylcholine receptor subunit genes that prolong channel opening.
Characteristically produces selective, severe weakness and wasting of the cervical, wrist and finger extensor muscles, an unusual pattern for a neuromuscular junction disorder.
Inheritance is autosomal dominant, so a family history of similar weakness across generations is a useful clue.
Cholinesterase inhibitors are contraindicated because they further prolong acetylcholine action and worsen the excitotoxic endplate damage.
Long-lived open-channel blockers such as fluoxetine or quinidine are the mainstay of treatment as they shorten channel open time.
Onset and severity are highly variable, ranging from infancy to adult life, and progression can be slow over decades.
A repetitive compound muscle action potential following a single stimulus reflects the prolonged endplate potential and is a characteristic finding.
reference.pathophysiology: Slow-channel syndrome arises from dominant gain-of-function missense variants in genes encoding acetylcholine receptor subunits, which alter channel gating so that the receptor stays open far longer than normal after acetylcholine binds, and may also show increased affinity and reopening. The prolonged and repeated channel openings allow excessive cation influx, producing a lengthened endplate potential that generates repetitive muscle fibre firing after a single nerve impulse. Over time the sustained calcium overload at the endplate is excitotoxic, causing degeneration of the junctional folds, loss of receptors, vacuolar change and an endplate myopathy, which accounts for the fixed weakness and focal muscle wasting rather than pure fatigability. Because the fundamental problem is excess rather than deficient cholinergic signalling, any intervention that increases or prolongs acetylcholine availability, including cholinesterase inhibitors, aggravates the calcium-mediated damage, whereas agents that block the open channel and shorten its effective open time reduce cation overload and improve strength.
additionalDifferentials: Fast-channel and other kinetic congenital myasthenic syndromes
Seronegative and acetylcholine-receptor-antibody-positive autoimmune myasthenia gravis
Distal myopathies and inclusion body myopathy given the selective forearm and finger extensor wasting
Motor neuron disease and focal amyotrophies
Endplate acetylcholinesterase deficiency, which can also worsen with cholinesterase inhibitors
additionalInvestigations: Repetitive nerve stimulation showing a decrement and a characteristic repetitive compound muscle action potential to a single stimulus
Single-fibre electromyography demonstrating increased jitter and blocking
Targeted sequencing of acetylcholine receptor subunit genes or a congenital myasthenic syndrome gene panel
Negative acetylcholine receptor and muscle-specific kinase antibodies to exclude autoimmune disease
In-vitro microelectrode and single-channel endplate studies where specialised facilities exist
Documentation of clinical response to an open-channel blocker and of worsening with cholinesterase inhibition
redFlags: Clinical deterioration after administration of a cholinesterase inhibitor
Progressive respiratory muscle weakness with hypoventilation
Rapidly advancing bulbar or neck weakness with aspiration risk
New severe distal weakness compromising hand function or airway protection
reference.prognosis: The disorder is usually slowly progressive over years to decades and can lead to significant disability, but open-channel blocker therapy often produces meaningful and durable improvement. Respiratory involvement warrants long-term surveillance.
pitfalls: Prescribing cholinesterase inhibitors, which characteristically worsen this subtype
Mistaking the selective forearm and finger extensor wasting for a distal myopathy or motor neuron disease
Overlooking the autosomal dominant inheritance and failing to evaluate affected relatives
Expecting pure fatigability and being misled by the fixed weakness and muscle wasting of the endplate myopathy
references: Standard neuromuscular and paediatric neurology textbooks
Peer-reviewed reviews of congenital myasthenic syndromes
